---
title: "Graphical Models"
---


A graphical model represents relationships among a set of variables as a graph. `bgms` estimates a class of undirected graphical models: pairwise Markov random fields.

## The idea in plain words

Take three things measured on the same people: trouble sleeping,
intrusive memories, and irritability. All three tend to rise and fall
together, so all three pairwise correlations come out positive. That
leaves the interesting question unanswered: which of these ties are
direct, and which only pass through the third variable? Perhaps
irritability tracks intrusive memories only because both are tied to
poor sleep. A correlation cannot tell you; it looks at each pair in
isolation.

A graphical model asks a sharper question for every pair: once you
hold all the other variables fixed, is there anything left between
these two? Each variable becomes a dot in a picture (a node), and a
line between two dots (an edge) is drawn only when the answer is yes:
knowing one variable still tells you something about the other, even
among people who score identically on everything else. No line means
that whatever association the pair shows in the raw data is fully
carried by the other variables in the model.

The picture that results is a map of direct associations. It does not
say which variable drives which: the lines have no arrowheads, and
the model makes no causal claims. What it does say is precise. Every
missing line claims that two variables have nothing left to say about
each other once the rest are known; every drawn line claims that they
do.

Two warnings keep the reading honest. First, "direct" means direct
among the variables in the model. Adding or dropping a variable can
redraw the map, because holding everything else fixed then means
something different. Second, a line missing from an estimated picture
is not by itself evidence that the association is absent; deciding
when the data genuinely support absence is a question of its own, and
answering it is much of what this package is for (see
[The Bayesian Approach](bayesian-approach.qmd) and
[Edge Selection](edge-selection.qmd)).

Everything below makes this exact: it defines nodes, edges, and the
mathematics that turns "nothing left to say" into a checkable
property of a joint distribution. If you would rather see the model
run before reading the theory,
[Getting Started](getting-started.qmd) fits one first.

## Nodes and edges

In a graphical model, the $p$ variables in a dataset are represented as nodes (or vertices) of a graph. An edge between two nodes indicates a direct statistical association between the corresponding variables, after accounting for all other variables in the model.

The absence of an edge between two nodes means the two variables are conditionally independent given the remaining variables. This is the key interpretive property of Markov random fields: the graph encodes the conditional independence structure of the joint distribution.

## Conditional independence

Two variables $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given the rest if $X_i$ provides no additional information about $X_j$ once all other variables are observed. In the graph, this corresponds to the absence of a direct edge between nodes $i$ and $j$.

Conditional independence is distinct from marginal independence. Two variables may be marginally correlated (both associated with a third variable) yet conditionally independent once that third variable is accounted for. The Markov random field separates direct from indirect associations.

## Markov Random Fields

A Markov random field (MRF) is an undirected graphical model in which the joint distribution factorizes according to the graph structure — it can be written as a product of pieces that each involve only connected variables. For $p$ variables with observations $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)$, the MRF specifies:

$$
p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(\sum_{i} \mu_i(x_i) +
\mathbf{x}^{\sf T}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\, \mathbf{x}\right)
$$

where $\mu_i(x_i)$ are node potentials that capture the univariate properties of variable $i$,
and $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is a symmetric pairwise interaction matrix.
The off-diagonal entry $\omega_{ij}$ is the partial association between variables $x_i$ and $x_j$. When $\omega_{ij} = 0$, the two variables are conditionally independent and the corresponding edge is absent from the graph. Thus, the primary inferential targets are the partial associations in $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ and the network structure that they imply.

## Model families in `bgms`

`bgms` estimates one general MRF. The variable types in the data determine the form of the node potentials $\mu_i(x_i)$ and the interpretation of the pairwise interactions $\omega_{ij}$:

- **Ordinal MRF** — all variables are binary or ordinal. Node potentials are category thresholds, and partial associations are proportional to log adjacent-category odds ratios. See [Ordinal MRF](omrf.qmd).

- **Gaussian graphical model (GGM)** — all variables are continuous. The partial associations are directly related to the precision matrix (inverse covariance matrix), whose standardized off-diagonal entries are partial correlations. See [GGM](ggm.qmd).

- **Mixed MRF** — for mixed discrete and continuous variables. The interaction matrix decomposes into blocks for discrete–discrete, continuous–continuous, and cross-type associations. See [Mixed MRF](mixed-model.qmd).

## Modeling conditional independence

The conditional independence structure — which edges are present — is typically unknown. `bgms` treats edge inclusion as a model selection problem, testing $\omega_{ij} = 0$ against $\omega_{ij} \neq 0$ for each pair of variables using spike-and-slab priors. This produces posterior inclusion probabilities that quantify the evidence for each edge. See [Edge Selection](edge-selection.qmd).
